name: Luke
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The earliest manuscripts of Luke are the papyri P75 (about AD 200–225), which preserves most of chapters 3–18 and 22–24, P4 (about AD 200) and P45 (3rd century); where they are cited in the notes, their readings are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Westcott and Hort printed in double brackets a number of short passages near the end of the Gospel that are missing only from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses (the so-called “Western non-interpolations,” including 22:19b–20; 24:3, 6, 12, 36, 40, 51–52), judging them additions; most modern editions, supported by P75, accept them as original. They are printed here in double brackets with a note. Passages found in later manuscripts but absent from the earliest witnesses (17:36; 23:17) keep their traditional verse numbers, and their text is given in the notes. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from the Greek of Luke, with the source given in a note. Money, measures and times of day are given in modern terms in the text (for example, a denarius as “a day’s wage”), with the original term in a note. The Gospel is anonymous; from the second century it has been attributed to Luke, the physician and companion of Paul (Col 4:14; Phlm 24; 2 Tim 4:11), who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:1). Most scholars date it about AD 80–90; others date it in the early 60s.

verses.text: Seeing that many have undertaken to set in order an account of the events that have been brought to fulfillment among us,
in keeping with what was handed down to us by the people who were eyewitnesses from the outset and who became servants of the message,
it seemed good to me also, having traced everything carefully from the start, to write it out for you in orderly sequence, most excellent Theophilus,{a}
in order that you might come to recognize how reliable are the matters in which you were instructed.{b}

In the time of Herod, king of Judea,{c} a certain priest by the name of Zechariah belonged to the priestly division of Abijah.{d} His wife, Elizabeth by name, was herself one of Aaron’s descendants.{e}
Both of them were upright before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and requirements of the Lord.{f}
Yet they were childless, for Elizabeth could not conceive, and both of them were well on in years.
It came about that, as he was carrying out his priestly duties before God while his division was on duty,
according to the custom of the priesthood, the lot fell to him to go into the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense.{g}
And all the throng of the people was outside, praying at the time of the incense offering.
There appeared to him an angel of the Lord, standing to the right of the incense altar.
Zechariah was shaken when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel told him, “Have no fear, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Elizabeth your wife will give birth to a son for you, and you will give him the name John.{h}
He will be a joy and a delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth,
For in the Lord’s sight he will be great. Wine and strong drink he must never drink,{i} and he will be full of the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb.
Many of Israel’s sons he will turn back to the Lord their God.

And he will go ahead of him in Elijah’s spirit and power, to turn fathers’ hearts toward their children,{j} and those who disobey toward the wisdom of the just, to have a people ready and prepared for the Lord.”
Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”
In reply the angel said, “I am Gabriel.{k} I stand before God, and I have been sent to talk with you and to announce this good news to you.
Look, you will be silent, unable to say a word, until the day when these things happen, since you did not trust my words, which will come true at their proper time.”
Meanwhile the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered why he was taking so long in the sanctuary.
On coming out he was unable to speak to them, and they understood that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He went on making signs to them and stayed speechless.
When his days of service were completed, he went back to his home.
Some time afterward Elizabeth his wife became pregnant, and for five months she kept out of sight, saying,
“The Lord has done this for me. In these days he has looked on me with favor, to remove my shame before others.”
In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town of Galilee named Nazareth,{l}
to a virgin promised in marriage to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.{m}
He came in to where she was and said, “Greetings, you who have been shown favor! The Lord is with you.”{n}
But she was deeply troubled at his words, and she kept wondering what sort of greeting this might be.
Then the angel told her, “Mary, have no fear; you have found grace in God’s sight.
Listen: you will conceive and bear a son, and Jesus is the name you are to give him.{o}
This one will be great, and he will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David,
and over Jacob’s house he will reign for all ages; his kingdom will never come to an end.”
But Mary asked the angel, “How can this be, when I have no relations with a man?”
In reply the angel told her, “The Holy Spirit will come over you, and the Most High’s power will cast its shadow over you. That is why the child to be born will be called holy, Son of God.{p}
And look, Elizabeth your relative has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren.
For no word from God will be without power.”{q}
Mary said, “Here I am, the Lord’s slave woman.{r} Let it happen to me as you have said.” And the angel departed from her.
In those days Mary set out and went in haste into the hill country, to a town of Judah.
She went into Zechariah’s house and gave Elizabeth her greeting.
And as Elizabeth heard Mary greet her, the child jumped in her womb, and Elizabeth became full of the Holy Spirit.
With a great cry she called out, “Among women you are blessed, and blessed is the fruit your womb bears!
And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
The moment the sound of your greeting came to my ears, look, the child within me jumped for joy.
Blessed is the woman who believed that the things the Lord has told her would be fulfilled.”

And Mary said,{s}
“My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior,

because he has looked upon the lowliness of his slave woman.
For look, from now on all generations will call me blessed,

for great things have been done for me by the Mighty One,
and his name is holy.

His mercy is for generation after generation
to those who fear him.

He has worked might with his arm;
he has scattered those who are proud in the thinking of their hearts.

He has pulled down the powerful from their thrones
and raised the humble high.

The hungry he has filled with good things,
and the rich he has sent away empty.

He has come to the help of Israel his servant,
remembering mercy,

as he spoke to our fathers,
to Abraham and to his offspring forever.”{t}
Mary remained with her some three months, and then went back home.
Elizabeth’s time to deliver arrived, and she gave birth to a son.
When her neighbors and family heard how the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, they shared her joy.
On the eighth day they came for the child’s circumcision, and they wanted to call him Zechariah, his father’s name.
But his mother spoke up: “No; he is to be called John.”
They told her, “None of your kin bears this name.”
Then they gestured to his father, asking what name he wished to give him.
Asking for a tablet, he wrote the words, “John is his name.” And all of them marveled.
Instantly his mouth was opened, and his tongue too, and he began speaking and praising God.
Fear came on all who lived around them, and throughout the whole hill country of Judea all these things were talked about.
Everyone who heard of it kept it in mind and said, “What will this child be, then?” For the Lord’s hand was indeed with him.
Then Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying,{u}

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,
because he has visited his people and brought about their redemption.

He has raised up a horn of salvation{v} for us
in the house of David his servant,
as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old:

salvation from our enemies
and from the hand of all who hate us,

to show mercy to our fathers
and to remember his holy covenant,

the oath that he swore to Abraham our father,
to grant us

that, rescued from the hand of our enemies,
we might serve him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High;
for you will walk ahead of the Lord to make his ways ready,{w}

to grant his people the knowledge of salvation
by the forgiving of their sins,

because of the tender mercy of our God,
by which the dawn from on high will visit us,{x}

to give light to those sitting in darkness and in death’s shadow,
to direct our feet into the path of peace.”
And the child kept growing and gaining strength in spirit, and he lived in the desert places until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

notes.text: Theophilus: a Greek name meaning “friend of God” or “loved by God.” *Most excellent* was a title of respect used for persons of rank (compare Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may have been Luke’s patron.
Taught: Greek *katēchēthēs*, “informed” or “instructed.”
Herod the Great, king of Judea under Roman authority from 37 to 4 BC. *Judea* here means the whole Jewish homeland.

Zechariah … Abijah: *Zechariah* means “Yahweh remembers.” The priests were divided into twenty-four divisions that served in the temple in turn; Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chr 24:10). *Abijah* means “Yahweh is my father.”
Elizabeth: Greek *Elisabet*, Hebrew *Elisheba* (Exod 6:23, the name of Aaron’s wife), probably “my God is an oath.” The meaning of *Aaron* is uncertain.
The Lord: in Old Testament phrasing like this, *kyrios* stands for Yahweh, as throughout Luke 1–2 where it refers to God (for example 1:9, 11, 15, 16, 17, 25, 28, 38, 45, 46, 58, 66, 68, 76).
Each morning and evening a priest burned incense on the golden altar in the holy place of the temple (Exod 30:7–8); a priest might receive this honor only once in his life.
John: Greek *Iōannēs*, from Hebrew *Yohanan*, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Compare Num 6:3; Judg 13:4; 1 Sam 1:11. *Strong drink* (Greek *sikera*) is fermented drink other than wine, such as beer.
Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew). *Elijah* means “my God is Yahweh.”
Gabriel: “God is my mighty one” or “man of God” (compare Dan 8:16; 9:21).
Nazareth: a small village in Galilee, not mentioned in the Old Testament; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
Joseph … Mary: *Joseph* means “may he add” (Gen 30:24). *Mary* (Greek *Mariam*) is the Hebrew name *Miriam*; its meaning is uncertain.

Greetings: Greek *chaire*, literally “rejoice,” the ordinary greeting. *Favored one* translates *kecharitōmenē*, “one who has been shown grace.” Many later manuscripts add “Blessed are you among women” (from 1:42); the earliest witnesses do not have it.
Jesus: the Greek form of the Hebrew *Yeshua* (*Yehoshua*, Joshua), “Yahweh saves.”
Or “the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God.” Some manuscripts add “of you” after “to be born.”
Or “For nothing will be impossible with God.” Compare Gen 18:14.
Slave woman: Greek *doulē*, the feminine of *doulos*, “slave” or “bond-servant” (also in 1:48).

Mary’s song (traditionally called the *Magnificat*, from its first word in Latin) echoes Hannah’s song (1 Sam 2:1–10) and many psalms. A few Old Latin manuscripts and some early writers attribute the song to Elizabeth.
Compare Gen 17:7; 22:17–18; Mic 7:20. *Abraham* is explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
Zechariah’s song is traditionally called the *Benedictus*, from its first word in Latin.
Horn of salvation: the horn is a figure of strength (1 Sam 2:10; Ps 18:2; 132:17).
Compare Isa 40:3; Mal 3:1. In the Hebrew text, the Lord is Yahweh.

Will visit us: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; many manuscripts read “has visited us.” *The dawn from on high* (Greek *anatolē*, “rising,” also used in the Greek Old Testament for the messianic “Branch,” Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8) may refer to the rising sun or star (compare Num 24:17; Mal 4:2).

verses.text: At that time an edict was issued by Caesar Augustus{a} for a registration of the entire inhabited world.
This was the first registration, made when Quirinius was governing Syria.{b}
So all were on their way to register, every one to his home town.
Joseph too went up out of Galilee, out of Nazareth town, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem,{c} since he belonged to David’s house and lineage,
to be registered with Mary, who was promised to him in marriage and was pregnant.
While they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth,
There she bore her son, her firstborn. She swaddled him and put him to lie in a feeding trough, since the guest room had no space for them.{d}
In that same region there were shepherds living out in the fields and keeping watch over their flock by night.
An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone all around them, and they were overcome with fear.{e}
The angel said to them, “Have no fear. See, I am announcing to you good news of a great joy, which is for the whole people.
For today, in the city of David, a Savior has been born for you, who is the Messiah, the Lord.{f}
This is to be your sign: a newborn baby, swaddled and lying in a feeding trough, is what you will find.”
And all at once there appeared with the angel a multitude of the army of heaven, praising God and saying,

“Glory to God in the highest heavens,
and on earth peace among people of his good pleasure!”{g}
After the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to each other, “Come, let us go over to Bethlehem and look at what has taken place, this thing the Lord has told us of.”
They went in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the feeding trough.
Having seen him, they reported the word that had been spoken to them concerning this child.
And all who heard were astonished at what the shepherds told them.
But Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.
Then the shepherds returned, giving glory and praise to God for everything they had heard and seen, all of it as they had been told.
When eight days had passed and it was time to circumcise him, he was given the name Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were completed,{h} they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”),{i}
and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”{j}
Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon.{k} This man was upright and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
The Holy Spirit had disclosed to him that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.{l}
Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple; and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what was customary under the law,
Simeon took him into his arms and blessed God, saying,

“Now, Master, you are letting your slave depart
in peace, according to your word,{m}
for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you made ready before the face of all peoples,

a light for revelation to the nations
and for glory to your people Israel.”{n}
His father and mother were marveling at what was said about him.
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, “Look, this child is destined for the fall and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against
(and a sword will pierce through your own soul too), so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare.”
There was also a prophetess, Anna{o} the daughter of Phanuel,{p} of the tribe of Asher.{q} She was far advanced in years. After her girlhood she had lived with her husband seven years,
and after that was a widow up to the age of eighty-four.{r} She never went away from the temple, but served God night and day with fasting and prayer.
Coming up at that very moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke of the child to everyone who was looking for Jerusalem’s redemption.
Once they had carried out all that the law of the Lord required, they went back into Galilee, to Nazareth, their town.
The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.
Each year his parents would go to Jerusalem for the Passover feast.
When he was twelve years old, they went up as the custom of the festival required.
After the days were over, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.
Thinking he was in the traveling party, they went a day’s journey and then began searching for him among their relatives and acquaintances.
Not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem to look for him.
Three days later they found him in the temple, seated in the midst of the teachers, both listening to them and putting questions to them.
Everyone who heard him was amazed by his insight and by the answers he gave.
His parents were astonished to see him, and his mother said, “Child, why have you treated us so? Here your father and I have been anxiously seeking you.”
“Why did you look for me?” he said to them. “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?”{s}
But they did not understand the saying he spoke to them.
And he went down with them to Nazareth and was subject to them. His mother kept all these words in her heart.
And Jesus kept advancing in wisdom and in stature,{t} and in favor with God and people.

notes.text: Caesar Augustus: Octavian, the first Roman emperor (31 BC–AD 14). *Augustus*, “revered,” was a title given him by the Roman Senate in 27 BC.

Quirinius: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, Roman legate of Syria from AD 6, when he conducted a census of Judea (compare Acts 5:37). How this registration relates to the reign of Herod (1:5) is a long-debated historical question; some render “this registration took place before Quirinius was governing Syria.” Scholarly review recommended.
Bethlehem: “house of bread,” David’s hometown (1 Sam 16:1; Mic 5:2).

Guest room: Greek *katalyma*, a lodging place or guest room (used of the upper room in 22:11), not necessarily an inn. The *feeding trough* (traditionally “manger”) suggests the part of the house or shelter where animals were kept.
An angel of the Lord … the glory of the Lord: in Old Testament phrasing, the angel and glory of Yahweh.
The Messiah, the Lord: Greek *christos kyrios*, “anointed Lord.” A few witnesses read “the Lord’s Messiah,” as in 2:26.

People of his good pleasure: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, first hands, and Codex Bezae), which read *eudokias*, “of good pleasure,” meaning people on whom God’s favor rests. Most later manuscripts read *eudokia*, giving “peace on earth, good will toward people.”
The purification of a mother after childbirth (Lev 12:1–8) and the redemption of a firstborn son (Exod 13:2, 12–15; Num 18:15–16). *Moses* is explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out.”
Exod 13:2, 12. In the Hebrew text, the Lord is Yahweh; the phrase *the law of the Lord* likewise means the law of Yahweh (also 2:24, 39).
Lev 12:8, the offering allowed to those who could not afford a lamb.
Simeon: Hebrew *Shimon*, linked with “hear” (Gen 29:33).
The Lord’s Messiah: literally “the Lord’s anointed,” an Old Testament phrase for the king chosen by Yahweh (1 Sam 24:6; Ps 2:2).
Simeon’s song is traditionally called the *Nunc Dimittis*, from its first words in Latin. *Master* is Greek *despotēs*.
Anna: Hebrew *Hannah*, “grace” or “favor” (1 Sam 1:2).
Phanuel: a form of *Penuel*, “face of God” (Gen 32:30–31).
Asher: “happy” or “blessed” (Gen 30:13). The tribe belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel.
Or “had been a widow for eighty-four years.”
Or “about my Father’s affairs”; literally “in the things of my Father.”
Or “in age.” Compare 1 Sam 2:26.

verses.text: It was the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar.{a} Pontius Pilate was the governor of Judea;{b} Herod was the tetrarch of Galilee,{c} his brother Philip the tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene.{d}
during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas,{e} the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
And he came into the whole area around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance that leads to forgiveness of sins,
and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’”{g}
So he would say to the crowds who came out to be baptized by him, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to escape from the coming wrath?

Then produce fruit that befits repentance. And do not begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.
Even now the ax is lying at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”
The crowds kept asking him, “What then should we do?”
He answered them, “Whoever has two tunics{h} should share with the one who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.”
Tax collectors{i} also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what should we do?”
He answered them, “Exact nothing beyond the amount you are directed to collect.”
Soldiers also kept asking him, “And we, what should we do?” He told them, “Do not take money from anyone by force or by false accusation, and be content with your pay.”
As the people were in expectation, and all were wondering in their hearts about John, whether he might perhaps be the Messiah,
John answered them all, “I baptize you with water; but one is coming who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.
His winnowing shovel{j} is in his hand, to clean out his threshing floor completely and to gather the wheat into his granary; but the chaff he will burn in a fire that is never put out.”
So with many other words of exhortation he proclaimed the good news to the people.
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been rebuked by him on account of Herodias, his brother’s wife,{k} and on account of all the evil things Herod had done,
added this to them all: he shut John up in prison.
Now when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit came down on him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: “You are my Son, the Beloved; in you I take delight.”{l}
Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began. He was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, the son of Heli,{m}
the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai,
the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda,
the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri,
the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er,
the son of Jesus,{n} the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi,
the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim,
the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
the son of Jesse, the son of Obed,{o} the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon,
the son of Admin, the son of Arni,{p} the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah,
the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah,
the son of Cainan,{q} the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech,
the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan,
the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.{r}

notes.text: Tiberius Caesar: Roman emperor AD 14–37. His fifteenth year was probably AD 28–29, depending on how the years were reckoned.
Pontius Pilate: Roman prefect of Judea AD 26–36.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. A *tetrarch* (“ruler of a fourth”) was a minor ruler under Roman authority.
Philip, another son of Herod the Great, ruled the territories northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Lysanias ruled Abilene, northwest of Damascus; he is otherwise known from an inscription.
Annas was high priest AD 6–15 and remained influential; Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was high priest AD 18–36 (John 18:13). *Caiaphas* is a family name of uncertain meaning.
Isaiah: “Yahweh is salvation.”
Isa 40:3–5, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Tunics: the *chitōn* was a garment worn next to the skin, under the outer cloak.
Tax collectors: men who collected tolls and taxes for the Romans or for Herod, often despised as collaborators and extortioners.
Winnowing shovel: a wooden fork or shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind, which blew the chaff away.
Herodias was the wife of Herod Antipas’s half-brother (Mark 6:17 calls him Philip); Antipas married her after divorcing his first wife.
Compare Ps 2:7; Isa 42:1. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses read, from Ps 2:7, “You are my Son; today I have fathered you.”

Luke’s genealogy runs from Jesus back to Adam and differs from Matthew’s (Matt 1:1–16) between David and Joseph. The difference has been explained in various ways (for example, as Mary’s line, or by levirate marriage); none is certain. The Old Testament names are given in their Old Testament forms where they can be identified.
Jesus: here the name of an ancestor; it is the Greek form of *Joshua*.
Obed: the Westcott–Hort text reads *Iōbēl*, with Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus; most manuscripts read *Iōbēd*, the Obed of Ruth 4:21–22. The same person is meant.

Admin … Arni: so the Westcott–Hort text, with some early manuscripts; the names do not appear in the Old Testament list (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr 2:9–10, “Ram”). Many manuscripts read “the son of Amminadab, the son of Aram” (compare Matt 1:3–4). The manuscripts vary widely here.
Cainan: this name appears in the Greek Old Testament (Gen 11:12) but not in the Hebrew text.
The son of God: Adam had no human father; compare Gen 1:26–27; 5:1–3. *Adam* means “human being” or “humankind.”

verses.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness
where for forty days he was put to the test by the devil.{a} Through those days he ate nothing, and at their end he felt hunger.
The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to turn into bread.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘A person shall not live on bread alone.’”{b}
Then the devil led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time.
“All this authority, and the glory of these kingdoms, I will give to you,” the devil told him, “for it has been given into my hands, and I give it to whomever I choose.
If you, then, will bow down in worship before me, it will all be yours.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.’”{c}
Then he brought him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle{d} of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,

for it is written,
‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, to guard you closely,’

and,
‘They will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot on a stone.’”{e}
In answer Jesus told him, “It is said, ‘Do not test the Lord your God.’”{f}
Having completed every kind of testing, the devil went away from him until a fitting time.
And Jesus went back into Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and word of him spread throughout the whole countryside.
He taught in their synagogues, and everyone gave him praise.
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and as was his custom he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day and stood up to read.
The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,
because he has anointed me
to bring good news to the poor.
He has sent me to proclaim release to captives
and recovery of sight to the blind,
to send away the crushed in freedom,
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”{g}
Rolling up the scroll, he handed it back to the attendant and sat down; and every eye in the synagogue was intent on him.
He began by saying to them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
Everyone bore witness to him and wondered at the words of grace coming from his lips, and they kept saying, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?”
He said to them, “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Doctor, cure yourself!’ What we heard had happened in Capernaum,{h} do here also in your own hometown.”
And he said, “Amen, I tell you, no prophet is welcome in his own hometown.
But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut up for three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land.
Yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in the territory of Sidon.{i}
And there were many with leprosy{j} in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”{k}
All in the synagogue, on hearing these things, were filled with fury.
They rose up and forced him out of the town and took him to the edge of the hill their town stood on, intending to hurl him over.
But he passed through the middle of them and went on his way.
He went down to Capernaum, a town of Galilee, and he was teaching them on the sabbath.
They were astounded at his teaching, because his word had authority.
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice,
“Ha!{l} What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.”
Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, it came out of him without doing him any harm.
Amazement came over them all, and they kept saying to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he gives orders to the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
And news of him kept spreading into every place in the surrounding region.
Leaving the synagogue, he went into Simon’s house. Now Simon’s mother-in-law was in the grip of a severe fever, and they pleaded with him for her.
He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. At once she got up and began to serve them.
As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.
Demons too were coming out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” He rebuked them and did not permit them to say anything, since they knew he was the Messiah.
At daybreak he left and went off to a lonely place. The crowds kept seeking him, and reaching him, they tried to hold him back so that he would not go away from them.
But he told them, “I have to announce the kingdom of God as good news to the other towns as well, for this is why I was sent.”
And he kept on preaching in the synagogues of Judea.{m}

notes.text: Devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer,” the Greek Old Testament’s rendering of Hebrew *satan*, “adversary.”
Deut 8:3. Many later manuscripts add “but by every word of God.”
Deut 6:13. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord your God” is “Yahweh your God,” as also in 4:12.
Pinnacle: literally “little wing,” probably a high corner of the temple courts.
Deut 6:16.

Isa 61:1–2, with a line from Isa 58:6 (“to send away the crushed in freedom”), in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh (Hebrew “the Spirit of the Lord Yahweh”). The *year of the Lord’s favor* recalls the year of release (Lev 25:10).
Capernaum: “village of Nahum,” on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.
1 Kgs 17:1, 8–16; 18:1. Zarephath was a Phoenician town; the widow was a Gentile.
Leprosy: the Greek word covered various skin diseases, not only Hansen’s disease (Lev 13–14).
2 Kgs 5:1–14. *Elisha* means “God is salvation.” *Naaman* means “pleasant.”
Ha: or “Leave us alone!” (Greek *ea*).
Judea: so the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts; here it probably means the whole Jewish homeland. Many later manuscripts read “Galilee.”

verses.text: Once, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.{a}
He saw two boats drawn up at the lakeside; the fishermen had stepped out of them and were washing their nets.
He got into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little way from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.
When he had stopped speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into deep water, and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered, “Master, we worked hard all through the night and caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the nets.”
When they had done so, they enclosed a great number of fish, and their nets were beginning to tear.
They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
Seeing this, Simon Peter fell down at Jesus’ knees and said, “Leave me, Lord, for I am a sinner!”
For astonishment had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish they had taken,
and so also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s partners. Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching people alive.”{b}
When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
Once when he was in one of the towns, a man appeared who was full of leprosy. Seeing Jesus, he fell face down and pleaded with him, “Lord, if you want to, you are able to cleanse me.”
He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
Jesus ordered him to tell nobody. “Instead,” he said, “go and let the priest see you, and bring the offering for your cleansing that Moses prescribed, as evidence for them.”{c}
But the report about him spread all the more, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses.
But he himself kept slipping away into the wilderness to pray.

On one of those days he was teaching, and sitting nearby were Pharisees{d} and teachers of the law who had come out of every village in Galilee and Judea, and out of Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was present for him to heal.{e}
And some men came carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.
Since the throng gave them no way of getting him in, they went up on the housetop and let him down through the tiles on his mat, right into the middle, before Jesus.
Seeing their faith, he said, “Friend,{f} your sins have been forgiven you.”
The scribes{g} and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Jesus, perceiving their reasonings, answered them, “Why are you reasoning this way in your hearts?
Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man{h} has authority on earth to forgive sins” — he said to the paralyzed man — “I tell you, get up, take your stretcher, and go to your home.”
At once he got up in front of them, picked up the mat he had lain on, and set off for home, giving glory to God.
Astonishment seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
After this he went out and noticed a tax collector named Levi{i} sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.”
And he left everything, got up, and began to follow him.
Afterward Levi held a great reception for him at his home, and many tax collectors and others were at the table with them.
The Pharisees and their scribes complained to his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
In reply Jesus told them, “People in good health have no need of a doctor, but the sick do.
I have not come to call the upright but sinners to repentance.”
They said to him, “John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers, and so do those of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.”
Jesus said to them, “Can you make the wedding guests{j} fast while the bridegroom is with them?
But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days.”
He spoke a parable to them as well: “Nobody rips a piece from a new coat to patch an old coat. If he does, he will have torn the new one, and the piece taken from the new one will not match the old.
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the new wine will burst the skins; it will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined.
New wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
[And nobody who has drunk old wine wishes for new; he says, ‘The old is good.’]{k}

notes.text: Lake of Gennesaret: the Sea of Galilee, named after the plain of Gennesaret on its northwest shore.
Catching people alive: Greek *zōgreō*, “take alive.”
Pharisees: a Jewish party devoted to strict observance of the law and the traditions of the elders. The name probably means “separated ones.”
The power of the Lord: here *kyrios* refers to God. Many later manuscripts read “to heal them.”
Friend: literally “Man” (Greek *anthrōpe*), a form of address.
Scribes: experts in the law of Moses, who taught and interpreted it.
Son of Man: an Aramaic expression meaning “human being,” used by Jesus to refer to himself, probably with reference to Dan 7:13–14.
Levi: “joined” or “attached” (Gen 29:34). Matt 9:9 calls him Matthew.
Wedding guests: literally “sons of the bridal chamber.”

Westcott and Hort placed this verse in single brackets as doubtful; it is absent from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses but present in the earliest manuscripts, including P75 (as reported in the standard editions), Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. *Good*: so the Westcott–Hort text; many manuscripts read “better.”

verses.text: It happened on a sabbath{a} that he was making his way through fields of grain, and his disciples were plucking the heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands, and eating them.
Some Pharisees asked, “Why do you do a thing not permitted on sabbath days?”
Jesus answered them, “Have you not even read about what David did when he was hungry, he and his companions,
how he entered God’s house and took the loaves of the presentation, ate them, and gave some to his companions, though no one may lawfully eat them except the priests alone?”{b}
And he told them, “The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.”
Another sabbath came, and he entered the synagogue and was teaching. There was a man present with a withered right hand.
The scribes and the Pharisees were watching him closely to see if he would heal on the sabbath, so as to find grounds to accuse him.
But he knew what they were thinking, and he told the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand here in the middle.” And he rose and stood there.
Then Jesus said to them, “Let me ask you something: on the sabbath is it lawful to do good, or to do harm; to save a life, or to destroy it?”
Looking around at all of them, he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He did, and his hand was made sound again.
But they were filled with senseless rage and began discussing with each other what they might do to Jesus.
In those days he went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the whole night in prayer to God.
At daybreak he summoned his disciples and selected twelve from among them, to whom he gave the name apostles:{c}
Simon, whom he also named Peter,{d} and Andrew his brother; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew;
Matthew and Thomas;{e} James son of Alphaeus, and Simon, who was called the Zealot;{f}
Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot,{g} who turned traitor.
He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a large crowd of his disciples and a great throng of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon,{h}
who had come to hear him and to be cured of their diseases. Those who were troubled by unclean spirits were being healed,
and the whole crowd was trying to touch him, for power was going out from him and healing everyone.

Lifting his eyes toward his disciples, he said:
“Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be fed until you are satisfied.
Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, when they cut you off and heap insults on you and throw out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man.
On that day rejoice and leap for joy, for look, your reward in heaven is great; it was in the same way that their fathers treated the prophets.
“But woe to you who are rich, for you are already receiving your comfort in full.

Woe to you who are full now, for hunger will come to you.
Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when all people speak well of you, for it was in the same way that their fathers treated the false prophets.
“But I say to you, my hearers: Love your enemies; treat well those who hate you;
bless those who curse you; pray for those who mistreat you.
To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other one as well; and from one who takes your cloak, do not hold back your tunic either.
Give to everyone who asks of you, and from one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back.
Just as you want people to treat you, treat them in the same way.
“If you love those who love you, what thanks is due to you? Even sinners love those who love them.
And if you do good to those who do good to you, what thanks is due to you? Even sinners do that.
And if you lend to those from whom you hope to get something back, what thanks is due to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, so as to get back as much again.
No, love your enemies, do good, and lend, despairing of no one.{i} Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
“Do not judge, and you will by no means be judged. Do not condemn, and you will by no means be condemned. Release, and you will be released.
Give, and gifts will come to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing, they will pour into your lap.{j} The measure you measure with is the measure you will receive.”
He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man guide a blind man? Will not both of them fall into a pit?
A disciple is not above the teacher, but everyone, when fully trained, will be like his teacher.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but take no notice of the beam in your own eye?

How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck in your brother’s eye.
“For no good tree produces rotten fruit, nor again does a rotten tree produce good fruit.
Each tree is known by the fruit it bears. People do not pick figs off thorns, nor do they harvest grapes from a briar.
The good person brings out good from the good treasure of the heart, and the evil one brings out evil from the evil; for out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them — I will show you what he is like.

He is like a man building a house, who dug, going down deep, and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood came, the river burst against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built.{k}
But whoever hears and does not do is like a man who put up a house on bare earth, with no foundation. The river burst against it, and at once it collapsed, and the ruin of that house was great.”

notes.text: On a sabbath: so the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts. Many manuscripts read “on the second-first sabbath,” an expression of uncertain meaning.

The loaves of the presentation: the twelve loaves set out before Yahweh in the holy place each sabbath (Lev 24:5–9), traditionally “showbread.” See 1 Sam 21:1–6. *David* probably means “beloved.” Codex Bezae adds after 6:4 a saying about a man working on the sabbath.
Apostles: Greek *apostoloi*, “those sent out,” “messengers.”

Peter: Greek *Petros*, “rock” or “stone”; compare Aramaic *Kepha* (Cephas). *Simon* is a Greek name used for Hebrew *Shimon* (Simeon), linked with “hear.” *Andrew* means “manly.” *James* is Greek *Iakōbos*, that is, Jacob. *Philip* means “lover of horses.” *Bartholomew* means “son of Talmai.”
Matthew: probably “gift of Yahweh.” *Thomas* means “twin” in Aramaic.
The Zealot: Greek *zēlōtēs*, “zealous one,” perhaps for the law, or a member of the later anti-Roman party. *Alphaeus* is a name of uncertain meaning.
Iscariot: probably “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, though other explanations have been offered. *Judas* is the Greek form of *Judah*, explained in Gen 29:35 as “praise.”

In the Westcott–Hort edition the words that follow in 6:18 (“who had come to hear him … diseases”) are numbered as part of verse 17; the standard English numbering is followed here. *Tyre* and *Sidon* were Phoenician cities on the coast north of Galilee; *Tyre* means “rock.”

Despairing of no one: Greek *mēden apelpizontes*, which may mean “expecting nothing in return.” So the Westcott–Hort text; some manuscripts read *mēdena*, “despairing of no one,” which this rendering follows in sense. Scholarly review recommended.
Lap: Greek *kolpos*, the fold of a garment above the belt, used as a pocket.
Because it had been well built: so the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts. Many manuscripts read “because it had been founded on the rock” (compare Matt 7:25).

verses.text: When he had completed all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he went into Capernaum.
A centurion{a} there had a slave who was ill and about to die, a slave he valued highly.
Hearing of Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him with the request that he come and bring his slave safely through.
When they reached Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He deserves to have you do this for him,
for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us.”

So Jesus went along with them. But when he was by now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to tell him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not fit for you to come in under my roof.
That is why I did not consider myself worthy even to come to you. Just say a word, and let my servant be healed.
For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
When Jesus heard this, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that was following him, he said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”
The messengers went back to the house and found the slave restored to health.
Shortly after this{b} he traveled to a town named Nain,{c} accompanied by his disciples and a great crowd.
As he drew near the gate of the town, look, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A sizable crowd from the town was with her.
Seeing her, the Lord was moved with compassion for her, and he told her, “Do not weep.”
He came up and touched the bier, and those carrying it stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, get up!”
The dead man sat up and started talking, and Jesus handed him back to his mother.
Fear took hold of them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and, “God has visited his people!”
And this word about him spread through all Judea and all the surrounding region.
John’s disciples brought him a report of all these things. So John summoned two of his disciples
and sent them to the Lord with the question, “Are you the coming one, or are we to wait for someone else?”
Reaching him, the men said, “John the Baptist sent us to put this to you: ‘Are you the coming one, or are we to wait for someone else?’”
In that hour he healed many of illnesses and torments and evil spirits, and to many blind people he gave the gift of sight.

And he answered them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: blind people see again, lame people walk, people with leprosy are cleansed, and deaf people hear, dead people are raised, poor people have good news brought to them.{d}
And blessed is anyone who does not stumble over me.”{e}
After John’s messengers had left, he began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?
Then what did you go out to see? A man clothed in fine soft garments? Look, those in splendid garments, living in luxury, are found in kings’ courts.
What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the man of whom it stands written, ‘See, I send my messenger before your face, and he will make your road ready ahead of you.’{f}
I tell you, of all born of women, none is greater than John; yet one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”
(All the people who heard, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice, having been baptized with John’s baptism.
But the Pharisees and the lawyers set aside God’s purpose for themselves, since they had not been baptized by him.){g}
“To what, then, shall I liken the people of this generation? What do they resemble?
For John the Baptist has come neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
Yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”
One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table.
And look, a woman of that town, a sinner, learned that he was at table in the Pharisee’s house, and she brought an alabaster flask of perfumed oil,{h}
and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, and kept kissing his feet and anointing them with the perfume.
Seeing it, the Pharisee who had invited him said within himself, “Were this man a prophet, he would recognize who and what kind of woman it is that touches him, for she is a sinner.”
In response Jesus said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” “Teacher,” he replied, “say it.”
“A moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred days’ wages, the other fifty.{i}
Since neither had anything to pay with, he freely forgave both. Which of the two, then, will love him the more?”
Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he canceled the larger debt.” And he told him, “You have judged rightly.”

Then, turning toward the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I came into your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
You did not kiss me, but she, ever since I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.
For this reason I tell you, her sins, which are many, have been forgiven, for she loved much.{j} But one to whom little is forgiven loves little.”
Then he said to her, “Your sins have been forgiven.”
Those reclining at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”
But he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

notes.text: Centurion: a Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers; here probably in the service of Herod Antipas.
Soon afterward: or “On the next day,” according to many manuscripts.
Nain: a village in southern Galilee; the name may mean “pleasant.”
Stumble over me: or “take offense at me.”
Mal 3:1; compare Exod 23:20. In the Hebrew of Malachi it is Yahweh who speaks.
Verses 29–30 may be Luke’s comment rather than the words of Jesus.
Alabaster flask: a sealed jar of soft stone used for costly perfume.
Five hundred days’ wages … fifty: Greek “five hundred denarii … fifty.” A denarius was a Roman silver coin, the usual day’s pay for a laborer.
For she loved much: or “as is shown by her great love”; her love is the evidence, not the cause, of her forgiveness (compare 7:42–43).

verses.text: Soon afterward he was journeying through one town and village after another, preaching and announcing the good news of God’s kingdom. The Twelve were with him,
and certain women who had been cured of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, the one called Magdalene,{a} out of whom seven demons had gone,
and Joanna,{b} wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, and Susanna,{c} and many other women, who were providing for them out of their own resources.
When a large crowd was gathering and people from town after town were making their way to him, he spoke by way of a parable:
“The sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path, where it was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the sky ate it up.
Other seed dropped onto the rock, and when it came up it dried out for lack of moisture.
Other seed fell in among thorns, and the thorns came up with it and choked it.
And other seed fell into the good soil and came up and yielded fruit a hundredfold.” As he said this, he called out, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear!”
His disciples began asking him what this parable might mean.
He said, “To you it has been granted to know the secrets{d} of the kingdom of God, but to the rest it comes in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’{e}
“Now the parable means this: the seed is God’s word.
Those along the path are the ones who hear; then the devil comes and carries off the word from their hearts, lest they believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are the ones who, on hearing, welcome the word with joy; but these have no root. They believe for a while, and in a time of testing they fall away.
As for what fell among the thorns, these are the ones who have heard, but as they go their way they are choked by cares and riches and life’s pleasures, and their fruit never ripens.
But the seed in the fine soil stands for people who, having heard the word, keep it fast in a noble and good heart and bear fruit through endurance.
“Nobody, after lighting a lamp, hides it under a jar or sets it beneath a bed; instead he sets it on a lampstand, so that those coming in may see the light.
For there is nothing hidden that will not become plain, nor anything secret that will not be known and come out into the open.
Pay attention, then, to how you hear. More will be given to anyone who has; and from anyone who lacks, even what he supposes he has will be taken away.”
His mother and his brothers came to him, but because of the crowd they could not get near him.
Someone reported to him, “Your mother and brothers are outside and would like to see you.”
But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these: the people who hear God’s word and do it.”
It happened one day that he boarded a boat with his disciples and said to them, “Let us cross over to the far side of the lake.” So they set out.
As they sailed, he fell asleep. A windstorm swept down on the lake, and they were taking on water and were in danger.
They went and roused him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” He woke and rebuked the wind and the surging water; they ceased, and all was calm.
He said to them, “Where is your faith?” Frightened and amazed, they said to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?”
They sailed down to the region of the Gerasenes,{f} which lies across from Galilee.
As he stepped out on land, a man from the town who had demons came to meet him. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he lived not in a house but among the tombs.
Seeing Jesus, he shrieked and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me!”

For Jesus had been ordering the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Again and again it had taken hold of him; they would guard him, binding him with chains and fetters, yet he would snap the restraints and be driven off into the desert by the demon.
Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,”{g} because many demons had gone into him.
And they kept begging him not to order them to depart into the abyss.{h}
A sizable herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and the demons begged him to let them enter these, and he gave them leave.
The demons came out of the man and went into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned.
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and spread the news in the town and in the countryside.
People went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
The eyewitnesses reported to them how the man who had been possessed by demons was rescued.
Then the whole population of the surrounding region of the Gerasenes asked him to go away from them, for they were gripped by great fear. So he got into the boat and went back.
The man from whom the demons had gone out kept begging to be allowed to stay with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying,
“Return to your house, and recount everything God has done for you.” And he went off, proclaiming throughout the whole town all that Jesus had done for him.
When Jesus came back, the crowd gave him a welcome, since everyone was expecting him.
And look, a man named Jairus{i} came; he was a leader of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he pleaded with him to come to his house,
because his only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. As Jesus went, the crowds were pressing in on him.
A woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years and could not be healed by anyone.{j}
Coming up behind him, she touched the fringe{k} of his cloak, and her flow of blood stopped instantly.
“Who touched me?” Jesus asked. As they all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds are pressing around you and jostling you.”{l}
But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceived that power had gone out from me.”
Seeing that she had not escaped notice, the woman came trembling and fell down before him, and in the presence of all the people she told why she had touched him and how she had been healed at once.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
He was still talking when a man arrived from the house of the synagogue leader, saying, “Your daughter has died. Bother the Teacher no more.”
But Jesus heard it and answered him, “Have no fear. Only believe, and she will be made well.”
When he came to the house, he let no one go in with him except Peter and John and James, and the child’s father and mother.
Everyone was weeping and beating their breasts for her. But he said, “Stop weeping; she has not died but is asleep.”
They laughed at him, knowing she was dead.
But he took her by the hand and called out, “Child, get up!”
Her spirit returned, and she rose at once, and he directed that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were beside themselves, but he ordered them not to tell anyone what had taken place.

notes.text: Magdalene: “of Magdala,” a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee; the name means “tower.”
Joanna: a feminine form of *John*, “Yahweh has been gracious.” *Chuza* is a name of uncertain meaning; a *steward* managed an estate or household.
Susanna: “lily.”
Secrets: Greek *mystēria*, “mysteries,” things once hidden and now revealed.
Isa 6:9.

Gerasenes: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus, P75, and others (also 8:37). Other manuscripts read “Gadarenes” or “Gergesenes.” Gerasa and Gadara were towns of the Decapolis southeast of the Sea of Galilee.
Legion: a Latin military term for a Roman unit of several thousand soldiers.
Abyss: Greek *abyssos*, the bottomless deep, here the place where evil spirits are confined (compare Rev 9:1–2; 20:1–3).
Jairus: Greek form of *Jair*, “he enlightens” or “he awakens” (Num 32:41).
So the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus and others. Many manuscripts add “though she had spent all she had on physicians.”
Fringe: Greek *kraspedon*, the edge or tassel of the garment (compare Num 15:38–39).
Many manuscripts read “Peter and those with him said,” and add at the end “and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

verses.text: Calling the Twelve together, he granted them power and authority over every demon and for curing diseases,
and he sent them out to herald God’s kingdom and to heal.
He told them, “Carry nothing for the road: no staff, no bag, no bread, no silver, and do not have a second tunic.
Whatever house you go into, stay on there, and from there move on.
Wherever people refuse to receive you, when you leave that town shake the very dust from your feet as evidence against them.”
They set out and went from village to village, spreading the good news and healing everywhere.
Now Herod the tetrarch heard of everything that was happening and was perplexed, since it was said by some that John had risen from among the dead,
some that Elijah had appeared, and others that one of the prophets of old had risen.
Herod said, “John I beheaded. Then who is this I keep hearing such things about?” And he was eager to see him.
On their return the apostles gave him an account of what they had done. Taking them with him, he went off by themselves to a town named Bethsaida.{a}
But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them and talked to them of the kingdom of God, and he cured those in need of healing.

As the day began to wane, the Twelve approached and told him, “Dismiss the crowd, so that they can go into the villages and farms round about to find lodging and get provisions, for here we are in a desolate place.”
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They answered, “We have nothing more than five loaves and two fish — unless perhaps we are to go and purchase food for this whole people.”
For there were about five thousand men. He told his disciples, “Have them recline in groups of about fifty each.”
They did so and got everyone seated.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
They all ate their fill, and what they had left over was gathered up, twelve baskets of pieces.
It happened once, as he was praying in solitude, that the disciples were with him, and he put a question to them: “Whom do the crowds declare me to be?”
They replied, “John the Baptist; but others say Elijah, and others that one of the ancient prophets has risen.”
He said to them, “And you, whom do you declare me to be?” Peter replied, “The Messiah of God.”
He sternly ordered them to tell this to no one,
saying, “The Son of Man must suffer much and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be put to death, and on the third day be raised.”
To all he said, “Anyone who wishes to come after me must disown himself, take up his cross each day, and follow me.
For whoever would save his life{b} will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake, he is the one who will save it.
What does a person gain by winning the entire world if he loses or forfeits himself?
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
I tell you truly, some who are standing here will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”
About eight days after these sayings, he took Peter and John and James with him and went up onto the mountain to pray.
While he prayed, the look of his face became different, and his clothing flashed white as lightning.
And look, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah,
who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure,{c} which he was about to fulfill in Jerusalem.
Peter and his companions were weighed down with sleep, but they stayed awake and saw his glory and the two men standing with him.

As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is a fine thing that we are here. We should put up three shelters, for you, for Moses, and for Elijah” — not knowing what he was saying.
While he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were frightened as they entered the cloud.
A voice came from the cloud: “This is my Son, my Chosen One;{d} listen to him!”
After the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent and in those days told nobody anything of what they had seen.
The next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.
And look, from the crowd a man cried aloud, “Teacher, I implore you, look on my son, for he is the only child I have.
A spirit takes hold of him, and all at once he cries out; it convulses him till he foams, and it will hardly leave him, battering him as it goes.
I pleaded with your disciples to expel it, but they could not.”
Jesus answered, “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long must I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.”
Even as the boy was coming, the demon dashed him down and threw him into a convulsion. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

And all were astounded at the majesty of God.
¶While everyone was marveling at all he was doing, he said to his disciples,
“Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands.”
But they did not understand this saying; it was veiled from them so that they could not grasp it, and they were afraid to ask him about it.
An argument started among them over who among them could be the greatest.
But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a little child and stood it at his side,
and told them, “The person who receives this child on account of my name is receiving me; and the person who receives me is receiving him who sent me. It is the smallest among you all who is great.”
John spoke up: “Master, we saw a man expelling demons by your name, and we kept trying to prevent him, since he does not follow along with us.”
But Jesus told him, “Do not prevent him. Anyone who is not against you is on your side.”
As the days for him to be taken up{e} were coming to completion, he set his face resolutely to go to Jerusalem.
He sent messengers ahead of him, and they went and entered a village of Samaritans{f} to make preparations for him;
but the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
When his disciples James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, shall we command fire to come down out of the sky and destroy them?”{g}
But he turned and rebuked them.{h}
And they went on to another village.
As they traveled along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.”
Jesus told him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have roosts, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
To another he said, “Follow me.” But he replied, “Allow me first to go and bury my father.”
Jesus told him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but as for you, go and spread the news of the kingdom of God.”
Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my household.”
Jesus told him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and keeps looking back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

notes.text: Bethsaida: “house of fishing,” a town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.
Life: Greek *psychē*, “life” or “soul,” also in the rest of the verse.
Departure: Greek *exodos*, “exodus,” here a reference to his death and what followed.
My Chosen One: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P45, P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus (Greek *ho eklelegmenos*). Many manuscripts read “my Beloved,” as in Matt 17:5 and Mark 9:7. Compare Isa 42:1.
Taken up: Greek *analēmpsis*, here of his ascension, and perhaps his death, compare Acts 1:2.
Samaritans: inhabitants of Samaria, between Galilee and Judea, who worshiped on Mount Gerizim and were at odds with the Jews (compare John 4:9).
Many manuscripts add “as Elijah also did” (compare 2 Kgs 1:10–12).

So the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts (including P45 and P75 as reported in the standard editions, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus). Many later manuscripts add, “and said, ‘You do not know what kind of spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people’s lives but to save them.’” Some include only the first part.

verses.text: Following these events the Lord designated seventy-two{a} more, and he dispatched them in pairs ahead of himself to every town and locality where he intended to go.
He told them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
Be on your way. I am sending you off as lambs into the midst of wolves.
Do not carry a money bag or a pack or sandals, and stop to greet nobody on the way.
Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house!’
If a son of peace{b} is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will come back to you.
Remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not keep moving from house to house.
Whenever you enter a town and they welcome you, eat what is put in front of you;
heal the sick who are there, and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God has come close to you.’
But if you go into a town where they refuse to receive you, go out into its open streets and declare,
‘We wipe off against you even the dust from your town that has stuck to our feet. Nevertheless, be sure of this: God’s kingdom has drawn near.’
I say to you, Sodom will fare more tolerably on that day than that town.
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!{c} For had the miracles performed among you been performed in Tyre and Sidon, long ago they would have sat in sackcloth and ashes and repented.
But at the judgment it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up as far as heaven? You will be brought down as far as Hades!{d}
“Whoever hears you hears me; whoever sets you aside sets me aside; and whoever sets me aside sets aside the one who sent me.”
The seventy-two came back joyfully, saying, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name!”
He said to them, “I was watching Satan{e} fall from heaven like a flash of lightning.
Look, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing at all will harm you.
Even so, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you; rejoice rather that your names have been recorded in heaven.”

In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for such was your good pleasure.
Everything has been entrusted to me by my Father. Nobody knows who the Son is but the Father, nor who the Father is but the Son, and whoever the Son wills to make him known to.”
Then, turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.
I assure you, many a prophet and king longed to see the things you are seeing, yet did not see them, and to hear the things you are hearing, yet did not hear them.”
Then an expert in the law stood up to test him. “Teacher,” he said, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God out of your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength, and with your whole mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”{f}
Jesus told him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
But he, wishing to justify himself, asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”
Jesus took this up and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho,{g} and he fell among robbers, who stripped him, beat him, and went off, leaving him half dead.
By chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.
So too a Levite,{h} when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a Samaritan who was traveling came upon him, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion.
He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
The next day he took out two days’ wages{i} and handed them to the innkeeper. ‘Look after him,’ he said, ‘and anything further you spend, I will pay you back on my return.’
Which of these three seems to you to have become a neighbor to the man who had fallen into the hands of the robbers?”
He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus told him, “Go, and you do the same.”
As they went on their way, he entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha{j} welcomed him into her house.
She had a sister named Mary, who seated herself by the Lord’s feet and was listening to his word.

Martha, however, was pulled in many directions by all the serving. She came over and said, “Lord, does it not matter to you that my sister has abandoned me to do the serving by myself? Tell her to lend me a hand.”
The Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things;
but few things are needed, or only one.{k} For Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

notes.text: Seventy-two: so the Westcott–Hort text, which brackets “two” (also 10:17); the manuscripts are divided between “seventy-two” and “seventy.” Compare the nations in Gen 10, numbered seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek Old Testament.
A son of peace: a Hebrew idiom for a person disposed to peace or worthy of it.
Chorazin … Bethsaida: towns near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. The meaning of *Chorazin* is uncertain.
Hades: Greek *hadēs*, the realm of the dead, corresponding to Hebrew *Sheol*. Compare Isa 14:13–15.
Satan: Hebrew for “adversary.”
Deut 6:5; Lev 19:18. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord your God” is “Yahweh your God.”
Jericho: a city near the Jordan, about 17 miles (27 km) from Jerusalem and some 3,300 feet (1,000 m) lower; the name may mean “moon city” or “fragrant.”
Levite: a member of the tribe of Levi who assisted the priests in the temple.
Two days’ wages: Greek “two denarii.” A denarius was the usual day’s pay for a laborer.
Martha: Aramaic, “lady” or “mistress.”

Few things are needed, or only one: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. P45, P75, and many manuscripts read “one thing is needed”; some witnesses omit the words “you are anxious … only one.”
